newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Jospin sheds "decent loser" tag - for now.
newsitem.headline: France's Jospin sheds "decent loser" tag - for now.

text.p: With the lefts surprisingly strong showing in Sunday's first round of the French parliamentary election, Socialist opposition leader Lionel Jospin has shaken off the "decent loser" mantle -- at least for now.

But to become prime minister after next Sunday's second round, the austere ex-education minister, 59, will need to turn widespread voter disaffection with the centre-right government into a mandate for his platform.

Polls show voters have little confidence in Socialist pledges to create 700,000 jobs, cut the working week from 39 hours to 35 with no loss of pay and set conditions for a single European currency which the Communist party rejects outright.

In a televised statement from his southwestern constituency of Cintegabelle, Jospin made a characteristically cautious and earnest comment on the first-round result, saying it showed a new, left-wing majority was now possible.

"I call on all those who want a more balanced government and a new policy for France to unite on this second round. All those who aspire to change must unite because a change of majority is possible and desirable," he said.

The first round showed that voters seemed to see their future on the left, he said. He promised if elected "a more audacious economic policy watchful of public spending, a more humane policy on social issues, a policy which will restart France, not for some but for all".

Criss-crossing the country in an aggressive campaign, the underdog Jospin revived his battered party as the uncontested main opposition force four years after it was decimated in a right-wing landslide.

The tag of "decent loser" earned in 1995 when Jospin gained a better-than-expected 47.3 percent of the vote in a runoff for the presidency against Gaullist Jacques Chirac, may become a distant memory.

For now, Jospin has turned his public image, widely seen as a liability, into an asset. A television puppet satire show long portrayed him as "Yoyo", a well-meaning simpleton based on Enid Blyton's "Noddy", driving round in a toy car seeking ideas.
While image-makers despair at his stilted, academic manner, untelegenic silver curls and rimless spectacles, polls have shown voters see him as more honest and genuine than his foes.

The tall, intense Jospin hammered away at Prime Minister Alain Juppe over record unemployment and political sleaze, and accused him of secretly preparing a new wave of austerity to make France eligible to join a single European currency from 1999.

But his fate hinges partly on how those who backed the extreme-right, anti-immigrant National Front, which according to projections won about 15 percent of the vote, transfer their ballots in the second round.

In his speech, Jospin said the Front's score was "high, too high" but offered its voters an olive branch, saying: "The next government must tackle as a priority the concerns of these French people, who are worried and who believe themselves forgotten and threatened, so as to answer their expectations."
Born in 1937 in Meudon, south of Paris, to a family of ardent Socialists, he had a strict Protestant upbringing in an overwhelmingly Roman Catholic country.
Like both Chirac and Juppe, he attended the elite National Administrative College (ENA) -- widely criticised for producing technocratic clones -- and then joined the Foreign Ministry.
Frustrated and bored, he dropped out shortly after the 1968 student revolt to become an economics lecturer and joined the Socialist party in 1971.
